title: Congenital Musculoskeletal Diseases
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)

overview.intro: This chapter covers inherited defects in the structural proteins that hold the musculoskeletal system together: fibrillin-1 in Marfan syndrome, dystrophin in Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy, type I collagen in osteogenesis imperfecta, types V and III collagen in Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and the growth plate receptor FGFR3 in achondroplasia. For each disorder the notes trace the path from gene to protein to the tissues that depend most on that protein, because that path explains the findings. Board vignettes give a body build, an eye or skin sign, a creatine kinase level, or a fracture pattern and ask for the gene, the inheritance, the complication that threatens life, or the look-alike condition that must be excluded.
prerequisites: Mendelian inheritance: autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked recessive patterns, penetrance, and expressivity
Collagen synthesis: Gly-X-Y repeat, hydroxylation, triple helix formation, and fibril assembly (MS-6, MS-8)
Skeletal muscle fiber structure: sarcolemma, basal lamina, and the contractile apparatus (MS-2, MS-7)
Endochondral and intramembranous ossification and the zones of the growth plate (MS-1)
Layers of the aortic wall and the role of elastic fibers in elastic arteries

connections.how: The dominant negative effect in collagen, the dystrophin reading frame rule, and the FGFR3 paternal age effect are developed there and applied clinically here.
Cystic medial degeneration of the aortic root in Marfan syndrome and arterial fragility in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome are causes of aneurysm and dissection.
Cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency in the methionine pathway explains homocystinuria, the main look-alike of Marfan syndrome.
Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is also classified as a genetic skin disease because skin hyperextensibility and fragility are its defining signs.
Dystrophin loss in cardiac muscle causes dilated cardiomyopathy, and weakness of the diaphragm and chest wall causes restrictive ventilatory failure.

sections.title: Marfan syndrome: fibrillin-1, TGF-beta, and the skeletal and ocular findings

blocks.text: Fibrillin-1 is a large cysteine-rich glycoprotein secreted by fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells. It polymerizes into microfibrils (about 10 nm wide) that do three jobs. They form the scaffold on which tropoelastin is laid down to make elastic fibers, so they are abundant in the aortic media, ligaments, and joint capsules. They act as structural cables in their own right, most importantly in the ciliary zonules that suspend the lens. They also bind latent TGF-beta through latent TGF-beta binding proteins, which keeps this growth factor stored in an inactive form within the matrix.

Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in FBN1 on chromosome 15 and is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Most mutations are missense changes whose abnormal monomers enter microfibrils and disrupt them (a dominant negative effect); others lower the amount of fibrillin made. The result is twofold. Microfibrils are mechanically weak, and they can no longer hold latent TGF-beta in the matrix, so more of it is activated, which raises local signaling, increases matrix metalloproteinase activity, and further degrades the matrix. Loeys-Dietz syndrome, caused by mutations in TGF-beta receptor genes, produces similar aortic disease, which supports a central role for this pathway.

Penetrance is high, but expressivity varies widely, even within a family, and the single gene affects many organs (pleiotropy). About one quarter of cases arise from new mutations, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis. Prevalence is about 1 in 5,000.
Skeletal and ocular findings

Long bones overgrow, so patients are tall with limbs out of proportion to the trunk: arm span exceeds height (ratio above about 1.05) and the upper to lower body segment ratio is reduced. Overgrowth of the ribs pushes the sternum in or out (pectus excavatum or carinatum). Lax ligaments and capsules give joint hypermobility, and the spine often curves (scoliosis). The cause of overgrowth is not fully settled; altered growth factor signaling around the growth plate is the leading explanation. Because the ciliary zonules are made of fibrillin microfibrils, they stretch and break, and the lens usually shifts upward and outward (superotemporal ectopia lentis), typically in both eyes.

rows: Arm span greater than height; low upper to lower segment ratio
Thumb tip passes the ulnar border of the fist (thumb sign); thumb and fifth finger overlap around the opposite wrist (wrist sign)
Overgrowth of tubular bones of the hands and feet
Lax joints, collapsed arches, spinal curve

blocks.caption: Every finding follows from tissue that depends on fibrillin microfibrils for strength or from excess TGF-beta signaling.

blocks.text: The revised Ghent criteria make aortic root dilation and ectopia lentis the two cardinal features; together they establish the diagnosis even without a family history, and aortic root dilation with a pathogenic FBN1 variant also suffices.

sections.title: Marfan cardiovascular disease and the homocystinuria look-alike

blocks.text: The aortic root, at the sinuses of Valsalva, takes the full pulsatile force of each ejection and depends on fibrillin-scaffolded elastic lamellae to absorb it. In Marfan syndrome the media shows cystic medial degeneration: elastic lamellae fragment, smooth muscle cells are lost, and pools of proteoglycan collect between them. The weakened root dilates, and by the law of Laplace (wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by wall thickness) each increase in radius raises wall stress further, so dilation tends to progress.

blocks.title: From FBN1 mutation to aortic dissection
steps: FBN1 mutation yields defective fibrillin-1 microfibrils
Elastic lamellae lose their scaffold; latent TGF-beta is released
Excess TGF-beta signaling and proteases degrade the aortic media
Aortic root dilates under pulsatile stress
Annular stretch causes aortic regurgitation
Intimal tear lets blood split the media: dissection
blocks.caption: Dilation raises wall stress (Laplace), so root enlargement is self-reinforcing until regurgitation or dissection occurs.

blocks.text: Three complications follow. Stretching of the aortic annulus pulls the cusps apart, causing aortic regurgitation, heard as an early diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure. A tear in the intima lets blood dissect along the weakened media, usually starting in the ascending aorta; rupture into the pericardium causes tamponade, and dissection is the leading cause of death. Pregnancy raises the risk because cardiac output and blood volume rise. The mitral leaflets undergo myxomatous change, become redundant, and prolapse into the left atrium in systole, producing a midsystolic click, sometimes followed by a late systolic murmur of mitral regurgitation.
Homocystinuria versus Marfan syndrome

Classic homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive deficiency of cystathionine beta-synthase (CBS), the pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) dependent enzyme that joins homocysteine and serine to form cystathionine on the way to cysteine. Homocysteine and methionine accumulate in plasma, homocystine spills into urine, and cysteine falls. Homocysteine injures endothelium and promotes platelet activation, so arterial and venous thrombosis occur at young ages. Homocysteine is proposed to disrupt the disulfide bonds of cysteine-rich fibrillin, which would explain the tall, long-limbed build and lens dislocation, but the lens usually shifts downward and inward (inferonasal). Intellectual disability and osteoporosis are common.

blocks.title: Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria compared
rows: High plasma homocysteine and methionine; urinary homocystine
blocks.caption: A tall patient with a dislocated lens plus thrombosis or intellectual disability points to homocystinuria.

blocks.title: Worked example: tall teenager with a dislocated lens
blocks.text: A tall 14-year-old with long fingers has bilateral lens dislocation and needs special education. Last year he had a deep vein thrombosis. Step 1: tall build plus ectopia lentis suggests a fibrillin problem, so both Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria are on the list. Step 2: intellectual disability and venous thrombosis have no mechanism in Marfan syndrome, but both follow from high homocysteine. Step 3: predict the lens shifted downward and the plasma homocysteine and methionine are high. Step 4: predict the inheritance is autosomal recessive, so parents are usually unaffected carriers, unlike the affected parent in about three quarters of Marfan cases. The deficient enzyme is cystathionine beta-synthase.

blocks.predict: Two patients with Marfan syndrome have the same blood pressure, but one has an aortic root twice as wide. Which has the higher wall stress?
blocks.explain: The wider root. By the law of Laplace, wall stress rises in proportion to radius at a given pressure, and a thinned media raises the stress still further, so the larger root is closer to dissection.

sections.title: Duchenne muscular dystrophy: absent dystrophin and progressive fiber loss

blocks.text: Dystrophin is a 427 kDa rod-shaped protein that lines the inner face of the sarcolemma. Its amino terminus binds actin filaments, and its carboxyl terminus binds beta-dystroglycan, a membrane protein linked to alpha-dystroglycan, which in turn binds laminin in the basal lamina. Together with the sarcoglycans, this dystrophin-glycoprotein complex transmits contractile force from the cytoskeleton to the extracellular matrix and protects the membrane from mechanical stress during contraction. It also anchors neuronal nitric oxide synthase, which helps dilate arterioles in working muscle.

The DMD gene on Xp21 is the largest known human gene (about 2.2 million base pairs, 79 exons), which gives it a high new mutation rate; about one third of Duchenne cases are new mutations. Duchenne muscular dystrophy is X-linked recessive and affects about 1 in 3,500 to 5,000 male births. Large deletions account for most cases, and mutations that shift the reading frame or create a stop codon leave muscle with essentially no dystrophin (see C04 and MS-9).

blocks.title: From absent dystrophin to muscle loss
steps: Frameshift or nonsense mutation: no functional dystrophin
Actin no longer anchored to dystroglycan and basal lamina
Contraction tears the sarcolemma; CK leaks out
Calcium enters and activates proteases (calpains)
Fiber necrosis, then regeneration by satellite cells
Regeneration fails; fat and fibrous tissue replace muscle
Progressive weakness, cardiomyopathy, respiratory failure
blocks.caption: Repeated cycles of membrane injury, necrosis, and repair exhaust regeneration over years.

blocks.text: Boys are normal at birth, and walking may be slightly late. Weakness appears before age 5 and begins in the proximal muscles of the pelvic girdle. The child falls often, walks with a waddling gait, struggles with stairs, and may walk on his toes with an exaggerated lumbar lordosis. Gowers sign appears because the gluteus maximus and quadriceps cannot extend the hips and knees: the child rolls prone and climbs up his own thighs with his hands. The calves enlarge and feel firm, but this pseudohypertrophy is fat and fibrous tissue, not stronger muscle. Most boys lose the ability to walk before about 13 years.

Creatine kinase (CK) leaks from torn fibers, so serum CK is markedly elevated from birth, often 10 to 100 times the upper limit of normal, and falls later as muscle mass disappears. Biopsy shows variation in fiber size, necrotic and regenerating fibers, endomysial fibrosis, and fat. Cardiac muscle also needs dystrophin, so fibrosis begins in the posterobasal left ventricle and progresses to dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias by the late teens. Weak diaphragm and intercostal muscles, worsened by scoliosis after loss of walking, give a restrictive pattern with falling vital capacity, nocturnal hypoventilation, and eventually respiratory failure, which with cardiomyopathy causes death in early adulthood. Brain dystrophin isoforms explain the cognitive impairment seen in a minority, and smooth muscle involvement can slow gut motility. Female carriers are usually unaffected but may have raised CK, mild weakness, or cardiomyopathy when X-inactivation is skewed.

sections.title: Becker versus Duchenne: truncated dystrophin and how to tell them apart

blocks.text: Becker muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the same DMD gene, but the muscle still makes some dystrophin. The reading frame rule explains the difference. A deletion that removes a number of nucleotides not divisible by 3 shifts the reading frame, creates a premature stop codon, and the mRNA is degraded by nonsense-mediated decay, so no protein is made (Duchenne). A deletion of a multiple of 3 nucleotides keeps the frame, so the protein is shorter in the middle (rod domain) but keeps its actin-binding amino terminus and its dystroglycan-binding carboxyl terminus, and it works partially (Becker). The rule predicts the phenotype in about 90% of cases; the size of a deletion matters far less than whether the frame is kept.

Becker is less common (about 1 in 18,000 male births) and milder. Onset is later, often between ages 5 and 15 and sometimes in adulthood, progression is slower, and patients usually walk beyond age 16, often into adult life, with survival into middle age. Calf pseudohypertrophy, cramps, exercise-induced muscle pain, and myoglobinuria may occur. CK is elevated, though usually less than in Duchenne at the same age. Cardiomyopathy can be out of proportion to the skeletal weakness and may be the presenting or fatal problem.

blocks.title: Duchenne and Becker compared
rows: After 16 years, often adulthood or never
blocks.caption: Both are X-linked recessive; the amount and quality of dystrophin, not the gene, separates them.

blocks.text: Separating them in the laboratory

Genetic testing of blood is usually done first. Deletion and duplication analysis detects most cases, and sequencing finds point mutations in the rest. Knowing the exact exons involved shows whether the reading frame is kept, which predicts Duchenne or Becker. When a muscle biopsy is done, immunostaining with antibodies against dystrophin shows the protein at the fiber surface. In Duchenne the sarcolemma is unstained in nearly all fibers; a few revertant fibers may stain because a second somatic change restored the frame in those fibers. In Becker the staining is present but faint, patchy, or discontinuous. An immunoblot measures size and quantity: no band in Duchenne, and a band of abnormal size or reduced intensity in Becker. Age at loss of walking is the clinical tiebreaker when tests are borderline, with an intermediate group between 13 and 16 years.

blocks.predict: A boy has a deletion of three exons that together contain 312 nucleotides. Predict his dystrophin staining and phenotype.
blocks.explain: 312 is divisible by 3, so the frame is kept. He should make a shorter, partly working dystrophin, with faint or patchy sarcolemmal staining and a Becker phenotype, despite the large deletion.

sections.title: Osteogenesis imperfecta: defective type I collagen in every tissue that uses it

blocks.text: Type I collagen is the main organic component of bone, and it is also the dominant collagen of the sclera, dentin, tendons, ligaments, and dermis. Each molecule is a triple helix of two alpha-1(I) chains, encoded by COL1A1 on chromosome 17, and one alpha-2(I) chain, encoded by COL1A2 on chromosome 7. Glycine must occupy every third position (Gly-X-Y) because only glycine is small enough to sit at the center of the helix. In bone, collagen fibrils are the template on which hydroxyapatite is deposited: the mineral gives stiffness and the collagen gives toughness, so poor collagen makes bone brittle as well as thin.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is a group of disorders of type I collagen, and most cases (about 85% to 90%) are autosomal dominant mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2. Two mechanisms set the severity (MS-9). A null allele halves the output of normal collagen, giving the mild form (type I). A glycine substitution produces a chain that joins trimers with normal chains and kinks the helix, so most molecules are abnormal (a dominant negative effect); these give moderate to lethal forms. Slowed helix folding exposes chains to excess hydroxylation and glycosylation, and much of the abnormal procollagen is retained or degraded in the endoplasmic reticulum. Rare autosomal recessive forms involve proteins that modify or process collagen.

blocks.title: From glycine substitution to fracture
steps: Missense mutation replaces a glycine in the Gly-X-Y repeat
Mutant chains join normal chains in the triple helix
Helix kinks and folds slowly; chains are overmodified
Abnormal procollagen is degraded or forms faulty fibrils
Scant, poorly organized matrix mineralizes abnormally
Thin, brittle bone fractures with minimal trauma
blocks.caption: One mutant allele can damage most collagen molecules, which is why substitutions cause more severe disease than null alleles.

blocks.text: The findings map onto the tissues rich in type I collagen. Bones fracture with little force, beginning in infancy or even before birth in severe forms, and fractures become less frequent after puberty. Repeated fractures and soft bone cause bowing, short stature, vertebral compression, and scoliosis, and skull films show excess wormian bones. A thin sclera lets the dark choroid show through, giving blue or gray sclerae. Hearing loss usually begins in adolescence or early adult life; it is conductive at first because of ossicle fractures and fixation of the stapes footplate, and it often becomes mixed later. Dentin is largely type I collagen, so dentinogenesis imperfecta leaves teeth gray-blue or amber and translucent, with enamel that chips off the weak dentin. Lax ligaments give joint hypermobility, and thin skin bruises easily. Serum calcium, phosphate, and alkaline phosphatase are usually normal, which separates the disease from rickets and other mineral disorders.

blocks.title: Main clinical types of osteogenesis imperfecta (Sillence)
rows: Null COL1A1 allele, half the normal collagen
Hearing loss common; near normal height
Crumpled long bones, beaded ribs, small chest
Progressively deforming; most severe in survivors
Very short stature, dentinogenesis imperfecta common
blocks.caption: Severity rises from type I to type III among survivors; type II is lethal around birth.

blocks.text: Multiple fractures in an infant raise two main possibilities: inflicted injury and a bone fragility disorder. Physical abuse is far more common than osteogenesis imperfecta, which occurs in about 1 in 15,000 to 20,000 births, so the reasoning must rest on specific findings rather than on the number of fractures alone. Both can also coexist.

Fractures from abuse reflect forces an infant cannot generate alone. Squeezing the chest from front to back levers the rib heads over the transverse processes and breaks the posterior ribs. Shaking or yanking a limb shears the immature bone just under the growth plate, producing classic metaphyseal lesions, seen as corner or bucket handle fractures. Fractures at different stages of healing (fresh lines beside mature callus) show more than one event. Injury beyond the skeleton strengthens the case: bruises in a baby who is not yet mobile, patterned bruises, subdural hematoma, retinal hemorrhages, and a history that changes or does not fit the child's developmental stage.

Osteogenesis imperfecta leaves evidence in bone quality and in other type I collagen tissues. Blue sclerae, dentinogenesis imperfecta, wormian bones, generalized osteopenia, bowing, short stature, joint laxity, and a family history of easy fractures or early hearing loss all favor it. Each clue has limits. Healthy young infants often have bluish sclerae, and type IV disease may have white ones. Teeth cannot be judged before they erupt at about 6 months. A negative family history does not exclude the disease, because new mutations are common. COL1A1 and COL1A2 testing detects most dominant cases, and normal calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, and vitamin D help exclude metabolic bone disease.

blocks.title: Clues that separate inflicted injury from osteogenesis imperfecta

Long bone shaft fractures, vertebral compression, bowing
Several ages that do not match the history
Can also be multiple, but with a fragility history and minor trauma
Normal density, no excess wormian bones
Osteopenia, thin cortices, excess wormian bones
Blue or gray, especially type I
Bruises in a non-mobile infant, subdural hematoma, retinal hemorrhage
Easy bruising possible, no inflicted pattern
Fractures, blue sclerae, or early hearing loss in relatives
blocks.caption: Fracture location and associated findings carry more weight than fracture count.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 4-month-old with three fractures
blocks.text: A 4-month-old has a femoral shaft fracture after a reported fall from a sofa. Skeletal survey shows healing posterior fractures of the left 5th and 6th ribs and a corner fracture of the distal tibial metaphysis. Sclerae are white, bone density looks normal, and the family has no fracture history. Step 1: a 4-month-old cannot roll forcefully enough to break a femur. Step 2: posterior rib fractures and a classic metaphyseal lesion are highly specific for squeezing and shaking. Step 3: healing rib fractures mean an earlier, unexplained event. Step 4: no osteopenia, wormian bones, or blue sclerae. The findings favor nonaccidental trauma; teeth have not erupted, so dentition cannot help.

blocks.predict: Why are classic metaphyseal lesions so specific for abuse, while a midshaft long bone fracture is not?
blocks.explain: The metaphyseal lesion needs a shearing or torsional force across the fragile zone below the growth plate, which a young infant cannot produce alone and which shaking or yanking supplies. A shaft fracture can follow a real accidental fall or minimal force in fragile bone, so it does not discriminate.

sections.title: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: collagen defects in skin, joints, and hollow organs

blocks.text: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a group of inherited disorders of collagen structure or processing (the 2017 classification lists 13 types) that share three features: skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility, and tissue fragility. Which feature dominates depends on which collagen is affected and where that collagen matters most. Type V collagen is a minor fibrillar collagen that co-assembles with type I and controls when fibrils start and how thick they grow, so its loss disorganizes skin and ligament. Type III collagen forms thin, pliable fibrils in tissues that must stretch: arterial walls, bowel, uterus, and skin.

The classic type is autosomal dominant, usually from COL5A1 or COL5A2 mutations that reduce type V collagen. Electron microscopy shows collagen fibrils of irregular, variable diameter, many abnormally large, with cauliflower-like outlines in cross section. The skin is soft and velvety and stretches far but springs back when released, unlike cutis laxa, where loose skin hangs in folds. It splits with minor trauma and heals as wide, thin, atrophic scars over the knees, shins, and forehead. Joints are hypermobile and dislocate, and easy bruising reflects poorly supported small vessels, while platelet counts and clotting tests are usually normal.

The vascular type is autosomal dominant from COL3A1 mutations, often glycine substitutions that act as dominant negatives. It is the most dangerous form. Skin is thin and translucent with a visible venous pattern and bruises extensively, but it is not markedly stretchy, and hypermobility is usually limited to the small joints. Because type III collagen supports arteries, bowel, and uterus, these organs rupture spontaneously: arterial dissection or rupture, perforation of the colon (often sigmoid), and uterine rupture in pregnancy, which shortens life expectancy.

blocks.title: Selected Ehlers-Danlos types
rows: COL5A1 or COL5A2, type V collagen
Hyperextensible velvety skin, atrophic scars, joint hypermobility, bruising
Thin translucent skin, extensive bruising, arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture
Generalized hypermobility, dislocations, chronic joint pain; most common type
Infant hypotonia, progressive kyphoscoliosis, fragile sclera
blocks.caption: Classic and vascular types are the ones tested most; the enzyme defects show that faulty collagen processing gives the same picture as faulty collagen chains.

blocks.text: Three distinctions recur on exams. Ehlers-Danlos and Marfan syndrome share hypermobility, but only Marfan gives tall stature, lens dislocation, and aortic root disease from a fibrillin defect. Osteogenesis imperfecta is a type I collagen disorder of bone, whereas Ehlers-Danlos mainly affects soft tissues. Bruising in Ehlers-Danlos comes from fragile vessel support, not from a platelet or coagulation defect.

Long bones lengthen by endochondral ossification at the growth plate, where chondrocytes proliferate in columns, enlarge (hypertrophy), and are replaced by bone. Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3), a receptor tyrosine kinase on these chondrocytes, acts as a brake on both proliferation and hypertrophy. Bones that form by intramembranous ossification, such as the skull vault, and the periosteal growth that widens bones do not depend on this process.

Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia (about 1 in 25,000 births). It is autosomal dominant with full penetrance, and almost all cases carry the same gain of function mutation (G380R, in the transmembrane domain) that makes the receptor overactive, so it signals even without ligand. The brake is always on, so the proliferative and hypertrophic zones are short and endochondral bones grow little. About 80% of cases are new mutations, linked to older paternal age (MS-9); homozygous inheritance from two affected parents is usually lethal in infancy. Other FGFR3 activating mutations give a lethal form (thanatophoric dysplasia) and a milder one (hypochondroplasia), so the strength of receptor activation sets severity.

blocks.title: From FGFR3 mutation to rhizomelic dwarfism
steps: Activating FGFR3 mutation signals without ligand
Growth plate chondrocytes proliferate and hypertrophy less
Endochondral bones grow short; proximal long bones most affected
Intramembranous skull vault grows normally; skull base stays small
Short limbs, near normal trunk, large head, narrow foramen magnum
blocks.caption: Only bone made by endochondral ossification is restrained, which explains the disproportion.

blocks.text: The body is disproportionate. The proximal limb segments (humerus and femur) are shortest, called rhizomelic shortening, while the trunk is near normal in length. The head is large (macrocephaly) with frontal bossing because the vault grows normally, whereas the endochondral skull base is short, giving midface hypoplasia, a depressed nasal bridge, and a small foramen magnum. Intelligence is normal, although motor milestones are delayed by hypotonia and the heavy head. This disproportion separates achondroplasia from proportionate short stature, such as growth hormone deficiency or hypothyroidism.

Short endochondral skull base and facial skeleton
Trident hand (gap between middle and ring fingers)
Short tubular bones of similar length in the hand
Fibula relatively longer than tibia, plus lax knee ligaments
Small endochondral skull base can compress the cervicomedullary junction
Short pedicles and narrowing interpedicular distance down the lumbar spine
Recurrent otitis media, conductive hearing loss
Short, horizontal eustachian tubes in a small midface
blocks.caption: Adult height is about 130 cm (4 ft 3 in) in men and 125 cm (4 ft 1 in) in women.

integration.text: Every disorder in this chapter follows one rule: a defective structural protein fails first and most visibly in the tissue that relies on it most. Fibrillin microfibrils support the aortic root and the lens zonules, dystrophin protects muscle membranes that contract hardest (pelvic girdle, heart, diaphragm), type I collagen gives bone, sclera, dentin, and ossicles their strength, type III collagen supports hollow organs and arteries, and FGFR3 acts only where bone grows from cartilage. Inheritance follows the protein's role. Defects in structural proteins that assemble with normal partners often act as dominant negatives and are usually autosomal dominant, whereas enzyme deficiencies such as cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency or lysyl hydroxylase deficiency are usually recessive, and a large X-linked gene like DMD has a high new mutation rate.

Pathology and physiology meet at the complications that cause death: aortic dissection in Marfan syndrome and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, restrictive respiratory failure and dilated cardiomyopathy in Duchenne, and cervicomedullary compression in infants with achondroplasia. Single clues have limits: a negative family history does not exclude a dominant disorder with frequent new mutations, Becker disease can present as cardiomyopathy alone, and a Marfan-like build with thrombosis or intellectual disability points to a metabolic cause rather than a fibrillin mutation.

summary: Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant FBN1 (fibrillin-1) disease; weak microfibrils and excess TGF-beta signaling cause tall stature, arachnodactyly, arm span greater than height, pectus deformity, hypermobility, and upward lens dislocation.
Cystic medial degeneration dilates the Marfan aortic root, causing aortic regurgitation and dissection, the main cause of death; mitral valve prolapse is also common.
Homocystinuria (autosomal recessive CBS deficiency) mimics Marfan build but gives downward lens dislocation, intellectual disability, osteoporosis, and thrombosis, with high homocysteine.

Duchenne is X-linked recessive with absent dystrophin: onset before age 5, Gowers sign, calf pseudohypertrophy from fat and fibrosis, CK 10 to 100 times normal, and death from cardiomyopathy or respiratory failure.
Becker comes from in-frame DMD mutations that leave a truncated, partly working dystrophin; onset is later, walking persists past 16, and cardiomyopathy may dominate.
Dystrophin staining is absent in Duchenne and faint or patchy in Becker; deletion and duplication testing shows whether the reading frame is kept.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is defective type I collagen (COL1A1 or COL1A2): fractures with minimal trauma, blue sclerae, conductive hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta, and joint laxity; glycine substitutions act as dominant negatives.

Posterior rib fractures, classic metaphyseal lesions, and fractures of differing ages favor abuse; blue sclerae, abnormal teeth, wormian bones, osteopenia, and family history favor osteogenesis imperfecta.
Classic Ehlers-Danlos (type V collagen) gives stretchy skin, atrophic scars, hypermobility, and bruising; vascular Ehlers-Danlos (type III collagen) causes arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture.

Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant FGFR3 gain of function, mostly new mutations with older paternal age, giving rhizomelic shortening, normal trunk, macrocephaly, frontal bossing, and normal intelligence.

Age cutoffs for loss of ambulation (Duchenne before 13, Becker after 16, intermediate 13 to 16) follow common clinical convention; confirm NABNE usage.

Osteogenesis imperfecta incidence (about 1 in 15,000 to 20,000), the share caused by COL1A1 or COL1A2 (about 85% to 90%), and the expanded genetic classification beyond Sillence types I to IV vary between sources.
The Ehlers-Danlos classification was revised in 2017 (13 types); confirm whether NABNE uses the current names or older Roman numeral types.
Achondroplasia incidence (about 1 in 25,000), the share of new mutations (about 80%), and average adult heights vary slightly between sources.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: dystrophin-complex (actin, dystrophin, dystroglycan, sarcoglycans, laminin) and growth-plate-zones (resting, proliferative, hypertrophic, calcified zones).
